newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers turn the screw in wages row.
newsitem.headline: French truckers turn the screw in wages row.

text.p: French truckers kept up a crippling six-day-old blockade of about 30 towns on Saturday, turning the screws on the national economy to try to get employers to meet their demands for better wagers and working conditions.
A second night session of marathon negotiations in Paris with employers adjourned after six hours at 1 a.m. (0000GMT).
A trade union spokesman said some concrete issues had been discussed but achievements were "rather thin". Talks were due to resume at 2 p.m. (1300 GMT).

Haunted by memories of a damaging 24-day rail strike a year ago which badly dented his popularity, Prime Minister Alain Juppe called on both sides to end the dispute quickly and agreed that a Transport Ministry official chair the talks.
Unions earlier accused employers of failing to negotiate seriously and said the next 48 hours would be crucial.
Haulage companies said they accepted a truckers' demand to be paid for all working hours, including time spent loading, but unions said that concession was not new.
The protests showed the first signs of hurting the economy as tens of thousands of trucks blocked motorways and a dozen fuel depots.

The southwest, parts of the south and the Calvados region in Normandy were all badly hit. Petrol stations ran out of fuel in areas of Normandy and in Bordeaux, the southwestern city where Juppe is mayor. It has been singled out for the worst blockade.
Paris was barely affected, but truckers started blocking a motorway to the capital's giant wholesale food market in Rungis. Police said produce was still getting through.
Unions have said they would blockade Paris only as a last resort, adding that roadblocks 150 km (90 miles) around the capital would be more efficient.

Thousands of foreign truck drivers, mostly British and Spanish forced to drive through France between northern and southern Europe, were stranded in the roadblocks, sleeping in their cabs and running out of food and money.

French truckers in Bordeaux let dozens of exhausted Spanish and Portuguese colleagues through their roadblocks. They warned of a safety problem as the tired truckers embark on the long drive home and advised caution to motorists.

The London Foreign Office ordered consulates in France to help stranded British drivers with money and contacts with home. The Spanish embassy advised drivers to lodge complaints with French police in order to be able to claim compensation for rotting cargoes.
Former film star turned animal defender Brigitte Bardot urged truckers not to let livestock starve in the blockade.
The Association of Food Industry said the protest was starting to have serious consequences on the industry's logistics and called for a rapid settlement.
The opposition Socialist Party sided with the truckers, who say they are underpaid and hugely overworked because of cut-throat competition between haulage companies.
It said their demands for wage hikes, shorter working hours and the right to retire at 55 rather than 60 were justified.
